title: Minerals and Rocks
seo_title: Geology 12: Minerals and Rocks Worksheets (BC Curriculum)

standard_text: Earth materials provide a record of geological processes: mineral properties and classification, igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock formation, textures, and mineral deposits in BC. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Geology 12)
meta_desc: Free Geology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): mineral identification, rock formation and ore deposits. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A rock's texture tells how it formed.
key_sub: Silicates are the largest mineral group.
body_html:
How to think about it

Minerals are classified by chemistry: silicates (quartz, feldspar, mica), carbonates (calcite), oxides, sulfides and native elements. They are identified by hardness, cleavage, lustre, streak and specific gravity.

Igneous textures show cooling rate (coarse = slow, fine = fast, glassy = very fast). Sedimentary rocks are clastic (sandstone, shale), chemical or organic. Metamorphic rocks are foliated (slate, schist, gneiss) or non-foliated (marble, quartzite). BC has copper, gold, molybdenum and coal deposits.

Example

Which mineral fizzes in dilute acid?

A carbonate

Answer: calcite

Example

Gneiss has bands of light and dark minerals. What is this texture called?

Layers from pressure

Answer: foliation

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all rocks are made of one mineral.
  • Using colour alone to identify minerals.
  • Thinking marble is foliated.

faq.q: Why does obsidian have no crystals?
faq.a: Lava cooled so fast that crystals had no time to form.
A rock with enough of a valuable mineral to be mined at a profit.

items.q: What type of rock is obsidian?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What type of rock is sandstone?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What is magma?
items.e: Lava when it erupts.

items.q: What type of rock is marble?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: Which rock is slate made from when it is changed by heat and pressure?
items.e: Metamorphic rocks form from other rocks.

items.q: What type of rock is limestone?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: How do metamorphic rocks form?
c: Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
items.e: Marble, slate.

items.q: What type of rock is pumice?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: Limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground without melting. Which rock forms?
items.e: Metamorphism.

items.q: Which rock is marble made from when it is changed by heat and pressure?

items.q: What type of rock is conglomerate?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: Which rock is quartzite made from when it is changed by heat and pressure?
items.e: Metamorphic rocks form from other rocks.

items.q: Where are fossils most often found?
items.e: Heat destroys them.

items.q: Sandstone is heated and squeezed deep underground without melting. Which rock forms?
items.e: Metamorphism.

items.q: Mudstone or shale is heated and squeezed deep underground without melting. Which rock forms?
items.e: Metamorphism.

items.q: How does sediment become sedimentary rock?
c: Layers are squashed (compaction) and stuck together (cementation).
It is heated until it glows.
items.e: Over millions of years.

items.q: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
c: Weathering breaks rock down where it is; erosion carries the pieces away.
items.e: Then deposition.

items.q: What type of rock is schist?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What type of rock is gneiss?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: What type of rock is chalk?
items.e: Igneous: cooled magma or lava. Sedimentary: layers of sediment. Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure.

items.q: How did the rock of the Organ Pipes in Victoria form?
c: from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from mudstone changed by heat and pressure
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
items.e: The Organ Pipes in Victoria is basalt (igneous).

items.q: Why are the Earth's resources such as metal ores limited?
c: They are made again every year.
They took millions of years to form and are being used much faster.
items.e: Finite resources.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Moon forms after a giant impact
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts, or the first animals appear?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
items.e: The Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: In the formation of sedimentary rock, which stage comes straight after erosion and transport?
items.e: Weathering → erosion and transport → deposition → compaction → cementation.

items.q: In the formation of sedimentary rock, which stage comes straight after deposition?
items.e: Weathering → erosion and transport → deposition → compaction → cementation.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
items.e: S-waves cannot travel through it.

items.q: Why are pebbles on a beach rounded?
c: They have been rolled and knocked against each other by water.
items.e: Erosion.

items.q: Which rock fizzes when a drop of acid is put on it?
items.e: Carbonates release carbon dioxide.

items.q: In the formation of sedimentary rock, which stage comes straight after compaction?
items.e: Weathering → erosion and transport → deposition → compaction → cementation.

oxygen begins to build up in the air

items.q: How does an igneous rock form?
c: by heat and pressure changing another rock without melting
by layers of sediment being cemented
by magma or lava cooling and crystallizing
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: Benjamin soaks four rocks of the same size in water and weighs them before and after. Which result shows the most porous rock?
c: the rock with the biggest increase in mass
items.e: Porous rocks soak up water.

items.q: Olivia cools melted salol (a crystal-forming substance) on a warm slide and on a cold slide. Which gives bigger crystals?
items.e: This models granite and basalt.

items.q: Layer A has a shark tooth fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer A formed?
c: The area was once covered by ocean water.
The area was always covered by ice.
The area has always looked the same.
The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
items.e: A shark tooth fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by ocean water.

items.q: Is sandstone an igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic rock?
items.e: Sedimentary rock is formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together.

items.q: How do sedimentary rocks form?
c: layers of sediment are deposited, compacted and cemented
items.e: Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary.

items.q: A geologist finds a rock with bands of crystals and no fossils. Which type is it most likely to be?
items.e: Banding forms under pressure.

items.q: Layer A has a fish fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer A formed?
c: The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area was always covered by ice.
The area was once covered by water.
The area has always looked the same.
items.e: A fish fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by water.

items.q: Why does granite have large crystals but basalt has small ones?
c: Crystals grow faster at the surface.
Granite cooled slowly underground; basalt cooled quickly at the surface.
items.e: Slow cooling gives time for large crystals to grow.

items.q: How do metamorphic rocks form?
c: existing rocks are changed by heat and pressure without melting
items.e: Marble and slate are metamorphic.

items.q: Does the rock cycle always happen in the same order?
c: No. Any rock can change into any other type by different paths.
items.e: It is a cycle with many paths.

items.q: Layer D has a coral fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer D formed?
c: The area was always covered by ice.
The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area has always looked the same.
The area was once covered by ocean water.
items.e: A coral fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by ocean water.

items.q: How did the rock of Kata Tjuta form?
c: from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from layers of river sand pressed together
items.e: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate (sedimentary).

items.q: Layer C has a seashell fossil. What does this tell you about the area when layer C formed?
c: The area was always covered by ice.
The area was once dry land with plants or animals living on it.
The area was once covered by ocean water.
The area has always looked the same.
items.e: A seashell fossil is evidence that the area was once covered by ocean water.

items.q: How do igneous rocks form?
c: when layers of sediment are pressed together
when magma or lava cools and becomes solid
when rocks are heated and squeezed without melting
items.e: Granite and basalt are igneous.

items.q: Which of these is an igneous rock: limestone, mudstone, obsidian or slate?
items.e: Igneous rock is formed when hot, melted rock cools and hardens.

items.q: Which of these is NOT a fossil: a fern leaf print in shale, a fish skeleton pressed into stone, a seashell washed up today or an ammonite shell turned to stone?
c: an ammonite shell turned to stone
a fish skeleton pressed into stone
a fern leaf print in shale
items.e: A seashell washed up today is not the preserved remains of a living thing from millions of years ago.

items.q: Why is granite used for kitchen benches?
c: It is hard, strong and resists scratching.
items.e: Igneous rocks with interlocking crystals are hard.

items.q: Which rock forms when limestone is heated and squeezed?
items.e: Limestone is metamorphosed into marble.

items.q: What is lustre?
c: how a mineral shines in light
items.e: Lustre can be metallic, glassy or dull.

items.q: What kind of rock is the Organ Pipes in Victoria made of?
items.e: It formed from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns.

items.q: Ava's model shows igneous rock changing into metamorphic rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, igneous rock becomes metamorphic rock by heat and pressure deep underground.

items.q: Ava's rock kit has a sample of granite. What type of rock is it?
items.e: Granite is igneous.

items.q: Which rock type often contains fossils?
items.e: Layers of sediment can bury organisms.

items.q: Which energy drives weathering and erosion?
items.e: The sun drives wind and the water cycle.

items.q: Lucas's model shows igneous rock changing into sedimentary rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, igneous rock becomes sedimentary rock by weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation.

items.q: What is the rock cycle?
c: the slow processes that change rocks from one type to another
the path of a rolling rock
items.e: Rocks are constantly recycled over millions of years.

items.q: Chloe's rock kit has a sample of basalt. What type of rock is it?
items.e: Basalt is igneous.

items.q: Mei asks what energy source drives metamorphism (heat and pressure) in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Maya asks what energy source drives weathering by rain and ice in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Hana needs a metamorphic rock for a display. Which sample should Hana choose?
items.e: Metamorphic rocks include marble, slate, gneiss, quartzite.

items.q: Liam asks what energy source drives volcanic eruptions in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Ethan's model shows metamorphic rock changing into sedimentary rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, metamorphic rock becomes sedimentary rock by weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation.

items.q: Noah asks what energy source drives rivers carrying sediment downhill in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Does a rock have to melt to become metamorphic?
c: No. Heat and pressure change it without melting it.
items.e: If it melts, it becomes magma.

items.q: Emma asks what energy source drives melting rock into magma in the rock cycle. What is the best answer?
c: the sun (which drives the water cycle)
items.e: Interior heat drives melting and metamorphism; the sun drives weathering and erosion.

items.q: Maya's model shows sedimentary rock changing into igneous rock. Which process causes this?
c: weathering, erosion, deposition, then compaction and cementation
items.e: In the rock cycle, sedimentary rock becomes igneous rock by melting into magma, then cooling.

items.q: Kai finds a rock that forms when sediments are deposited in layers, then compacted and cemented. What type of rock is it?
items.e: Sedimentary rock forms when sediments are deposited in layers, then compacted and cemented.

items.q: What are the three main types of rock?
items.e: They form in different ways.

items.q: Emma's rock kit has a sample of shale. What type of rock is it?
items.e: Shale is sedimentary.

items.q: Ethan's model shows sedimentary rock changing into metamorphic rock. Which process causes this?
items.e: In the rock cycle, sedimentary rock becomes metamorphic rock by heat and pressure deep underground.

items.q: Kai reads about a resource that formed from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers). Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how groundwater formed.

items.q: Why is a cap rock needed for an oil or gas reservoir?
c: it is impermeable, so it stops the oil and gas escaping upwards
items.e: Shale and salt are common cap rocks.

items.q: Chloe reads about a resource that formed from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how copper and gold ores formed.

items.q: Ethan asks how oil and natural gas formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
items.e: Oil and natural gas formed from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years.

items.q: Emma asks how groundwater formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers)
from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
items.e: Groundwater formed from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers).

items.q: What is an ore?
c: rock containing a mineral in high enough concentration to be mined at a profit
a pure metal found in nature
items.e: Whether a deposit is ore depends on price and cost.

items.q: Lucas asks how rock salt formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers)
from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years
from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
items.e: Rock salt formed from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago.

items.q: Why can a deposit that was not ore become ore?
c: a rise in metal price or a cheaper mining method makes it profitable
the deposit moves closer to the surface
the metal grows in the rock
items.e: Economics defines ore.

items.q: How do oil and natural gas form?
c: remains of marine plankton are buried, heated and changed into hydrocarbons, which collect in traps
items.e: They need a source rock, reservoir rock and cap rock.

items.q: Why are fossil fuels called non-renewable?
c: they form over millions of years, far slower than we use them
they are found only in deserts
items.e: Coal, oil and gas are non-renewable.

items.q: Which method is used to explore for ore bodies by measuring small differences in gravity or magnetism?
items.e: Drilling then confirms the ore.

items.q: Noah reads about a resource that formed from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how coal formed.

items.q: When is open-cut mining used rather than underground mining?
c: when the ore is very deep and narrow
when the ore is large and close to the surface
items.e: The Super Pit at Kalgoorlie is open-cut.

items.q: What is a placer deposit?
c: heavy minerals such as gold concentrated by flowing water in river or beach sands
items.e: The 1850s Victorian gold rush was mostly placer gold.

items.q: Ethan reads about a resource that formed from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how iron ore formed.

items.q: Noah reads about a resource that formed from tiny marine organisms buried in ocean sediments, then heated and pressed for millions of years. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how oil and natural gas formed.

items.q: Ethan reads about a resource that formed from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how rock salt formed.

items.q: How does bauxite form?
c: intense weathering in a hot, wet climate leaches other minerals and leaves aluminum oxides
items.e: It is a residual deposit.

items.q: What kind of rock is Kata Tjuta made of?
items.e: It formed from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together.

items.q: What is mineral processing (beneficiation)?
c: crushing ore and separating the valuable mineral from the waste rock
items.e: Flotation separates many sulfide minerals.
